results.title: H100 Rental Prices Jump 22% in a Month as GPU Shortage Hits Firms and Labs - Seoul Economic Daily
highlights:
■ Surging GPU costs: Demand for artificial intelligence computing has climbed sharply, prompting domestic cloud providers to raise graphics processing unit rental rates following similar moves by U.S. neocloud companies. Unlike the past, when rental rates for older products fell as new ones arrived, prices for previous-generation GPUs are rising as well, making the ability to secure computing resources a decisive factor in the success of AI businesses and research.

...

[News of Interest to Corporate CEOs]

- Key summary: Vessl AI, a domestic neocloud company, raised the hourly rate for Nvidia H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39 on the 1st of this month, a 24.7% increase. The price adjustment marks the start of similar moves in Korea after U.S. neocloud firms including CoreWeave and Nebius successively raised GPU rental rates. Vessl AI procures most of its roughly 7,000 GPUs through leasing. According to Ornn, an AI computing trading platform, the hourly cloud rental rate for the H100 rose 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, reaching about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. The impact is spreading to industry and research, with some companies abandoning bids for government-led AI transformation projects because they could not secure GPUs, while universities and research institutes scale back the size of their research.

Take H100 pricing as an example.

In 2026, providers in our network have raised their H100 rates by an average of 31.6%.

results.title: H100 GPU Rental Cost Per Hour 2026: All Providers
highlights:
# H100 GPU Rental Cost Per Hour 2026: All Providers

Fazlur Rahman September 23, 2026· Updated October 27, 2026 9 min read

H100 GPU rental cost per hour 2026: cheapest verified rate is Vast.ai interruptible at $1.49/GPU-hr (July 2026); RunPod Community Cloud H100 PCIe at $1.99/GPU-hr; specialist-cloud H100 SXM at $2.99-$6.16/GPU-hr; hyperscaler on-demand at $6.88-$12.29/GPU-hr. Reserved-capacity contracts unlock 30-60% off list for predictable workloads.

Last verified: Sep 16, 2026.

## At a glance

> - Vast.ai marketplace floor: $1.49/GPU-hr interruptible (cheapest published)
> - RunPod Community Cloud H100 PCIe: $1.99/GPU-hr; SXM $2.69/GPU-hr
> - RunPod Secure Cloud H100 PCIe: $2.89/GPU-hr; SXM $3.29/GPU-hr
> - Lambda 1x H100 PCIe: $3.29/GPU-hr; H100 SXM $3.99/GPU-hr
> - CoreWeave HGX H100 (8x): $6.16/GPU-hr on-demand, $2.46/GPU-hr spot
> - AWS Capacity Blocks p5.4xlarge: $5.191/GPU-hr effective reserved
> - Azure ND H100 v5: $12.29/GPU-hr on-demand (highest)
> - GCP A3 a3-highgpu-8g: $11.06/GPU-hr on-demand, $3.69/GPU-hr spot

## Why H100 rental rates vary 8x for identical silicon

A verified H100 SXM ranges from $2.99/GPU-hr to $12.29/GPU-hr in 2026 — the spread comes from what surrounds the GPU.

Five structural variables move the rate: (1) instance size — 1x vs 8x node; (2) chip form factor — PCIe vs SXM (SXM runs NVLink at 900 GB/s, required for multi-GPU gradient synchronization); (3) included CPU/RAM/storage — bare accelerator vs fully provisioned VM; (4) billing commitment — interruptible spot vs on-demand vs reserved 1-3 year; (5) provider tier — marketplace host, neocloud, hyperscaler (answerfootprint.com, September 2026).

The cheapest rates come from hosts with the least overhead. Vast.ai's marketplace aggregates independent GPU owners willing to rent at $1.49/GPU-hr interruptible — the cost of interruptibility and host-level reliability variance. RunPod Community Cloud at $1.99/GPU-hr for H100 PCIe is next-cheapest because RunPod does not own the silicon; third-party hosts supply it. The most expensive rate — Azure ND H100 v5 at $12.29/GPU-hr — pays for compliance certifications, multi-region availability, and a 4-week capacity-quota approval process for 8+ node requests (cloudzero.com, September 2026).

## Specialist-cloud H100 pricing

Specialist clouds are the practical middle layer between marketplace rates and hyperscaler list.

Lambda Labs runs the most transparent published card with verified August 2026 rates: H100 PCIe 1x at $3.29/GPU-hr; H100 SXM 1x at $4.29/GPU-hr; H100 SXM 8x (208 vCPUs, 1.8 TB RAM, 22 TB SSD) at $3.99/GPU-hr (lambda.ai/pricing). Lambda Reserved Cloud 1-Click Cluster pricing drops further: 16-GPU HGX H100 at $6.16/GPU-hr; 64-GPU at $5.85; 256-GPU at $5.54 — all on 2-week to 1-year terms. Lambda's H100 capacity is intermittent: multi-week waitlists during demand spikes are the recurring complaint. The recurring complaint in 2026 is capacity, not price.

RunPod offers two tiers with the same hardware: Community Cloud (third-party hosts) at $1.99/GPU-hr H100 PCIe / $2.69/GPU-hr H100 SXM / $3.59 H200; Secure Cloud (RunPod's own datacenters) at $2.89/GPU-hr H100 PCIe / $3.29/GPU-hr H100 SXM / $4.59 H200. RunPod bills per-second (1-minute minimum). Storage is metered separately. The Community-to-Secure spread is the cost of platform-level reliability vs host-level reliability.

CoreWeave publishes an 8-GPU-node rate card, not per-GPU rates. HGX H100 8x at $49.24/hr on-demand = $6.16/GPU-hr; spot $19.71/hr = $2.46/GPU-hr (40-60% off on-demand). HGX H200 8x at $50.44/hr = $6.31/GPU-hr; spot $20.93/hr = $2.62/GPU-hr. The 8-GPU minimum is the real cost — single H100 is not bookable on CoreWeave at any price except GH200 (1x at $6.50/hr). Reserved contracts up to 60% off, all sales-negotiated. CoreWeave's business model runs on the third tier (OpenAI $22.4B cumulative, Meta $21B through 2032); the rate card is for everyone who hasn't negotiated yet (cloudzero.com, September 2026).

## Hyperscaler H100 pricing

At 8x node level, AWS, GCP, and Azure cluster within 15 cents of each other at roughly $98.32-$98.46/hr — but per-GPU normalization exposes a 4x spread.

AWS p5.48xlarge (8x H100 80GB, 640 GB total HBM3) lists at $55.04/hr on-demand, $41.528/hr effective under Capacity Blocks for ML (US East), $23.777/hr on 1-year Reserved, $19.769/hr on spot (vantage.sh, July 2026). Capacity Blocks require committing to a future time window — middle ground between on-demand and reserved. A separately-priced aggregator lists a single-GPU p5.4xlarge on-demand at $6.88/GPU-hr. AWS announced an 'up to 45%' price reduction on H100 in June 2025; the current effective rate is the result.

Google Cloud a3-highgpu-8g (8x H100) lists at $88.49/hr on-demand, drops to $38.86/hr on 3-year committed use discount (CUD) — a 55% discount versus list (gpusmith.com, July 2026). The newer a3-megagpu-8g with enhanced GPU-to-GPU networking runs $93.40/hr on-demand, $40.65/hr on 3-year CUD. GCP's a3-ultragpu-8g ships with 8x H200 (not H100) at $84.81/hr on-demand — confusing naming, worth verifying SKU. Spot pricing on GCP H100 runs $2.10-$2.80/GPU-hr depending on region.

Azure ND H100 v5 series (Standard_ND96isr_H100_v5, 8x H100, 96 vCPUs, 1.9 TB RAM) is the most expensive at $98.32/hr on-demand ($12.29/GPU-hr normalized) — consistent across July 2026 pricing surveys (vantage.sh, spheron.network). 1-year reservation brings it to ~$63.40/hr ($7.93/GPU-hr); 3-year reservation to ~$43.79/hr ($5.47/GPU-hr). Azure's quota approval process for 8+ node requests can stretch to 3-4 weeks before capacity is confirmed — a structural disadvantage for time-sensitive training jobs.

...

Verified H100 PCIe prices on Vast.ai: unverified community hosts at $0.90-$1.60/GPU-hr; datacenter-verified hosts at $1.50-$2.27/GPU-hr (spheron.network, July 2026). The Vast.ai 'on-demand' label does not mean what it means on AWS or GCP — it means the host is currently offering the machine at the listed price and will not actively evict you, but if the host takes the hardware offline for any reason, the machine stops. There is no platform-level guarantee of availability. For fault-tolerant training with checkpoint discipline, Vast.ai interruptible at $1.49/GPU-hr is the cheapest credible option in 2026.

...

## Reserved-capacity economics

For predictable training workloads, reserved capacity delivers 30-60% off list — but the headline rates are misleading.

Together AI's reserved cluster (91-180 day) starts at $3.09/GPU-hr for H100 SXM. Lambda 1-Click Cluster 16-GPU reservation drops to $6.16/GPU-hr on 2-week-1-year terms, $5.54/GPU-hr at 256-GPU scale. CoreWeave reserved capacity ceiling is 'up to 60% off on-demand' — target $2.46/GPU-hr reserved for H100 — but only achievable through sales negotiation. Hyperscaler 1-year reservations bring H100 to $7-$8/GPU-hr; 3-year reservations to $5-$6/GPU-hr (nOps FinOps, August 2026).

The break-even calculation: for a job that runs continuously for 6+ months, reserved beats on-demand even with the deposit. For a workload that might run for 2 weeks and then stop, on-demand wins because reserved capacity is wasted if unused. The reservation deposit on hyperscalers is typically 30-50% of the 1-year value, refundable only if you commit to a longer term. Most mid-market teams should avoid 3-year reservations unless they have locked-in demand.

## Side-by-side H100 pricing comparison

| Provider | SKU / Shape | $/GPU-hr | Billing | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vast.ai (verified DC) | H100 PCIe interruptible | $1.49-$2.27 | Per-hour | Cheapest; host-dependent reliability |
| RunPod Community | H100 PCIe pod | $1.99 | Per-second | Third-party hosts |
| RunPod Community | H100 SXM pod | $2.69 | Per-second | Third-party hosts |
| RunPod Secure | H100 SXM pod | $3.29 | Per-second | RunPod datacenters |
| Lambda | 1x H100 PCIe VM | $3.29 | Per-hour (1-min increments) | Transparent card |
| Together AI reserved | H100 SXM 91-180 day | $3.09 | Reserved cluster | Time-bounded reservation |
| Lambda | H100 SXM 1x VM | $3.99 | Per-hour | NVLink interconnect |
| CoreWeave spot | HGX H100 8x node | $2.46 | Spot interruptible | $19.71/hr node |
| CoreWeave on-demand | HGX H100 8x node | $6.16 | On-demand | 8-GPU minimum |
| AWS Capacity Blocks | p5.4xlarge single H100 | $5.191 | Reserved window | Future-dated reservation |
| AWS on-demand | p5.48xlarge 8x H100 | $6.88 | On-demand | $55.04/hr node |
| GCP on-demand | a3-highgpu-8g H100 | $11.06 | On-demand | $88.49/hr node |
| GCP 3-yr CUD | a3-highgpu-8g H100 | $4.86 | 3-year reserved | 55% off list |
| Azure ND H100 v5 | 8x H100 v5 | $12.29 | On-demand | Most expensive tier-1 |
| Azure 3-yr reserved | 8x H100 v5 | $5.47 | 3-year reserved | Best discount |

...

The decision hinges on three variables: workload duration, reliability tolerance, and budget.

1. For a 1-day fine-tuning experiment: Vast.ai verified datacenter at $1.49/GPU-hr. Accept interruptibility; checkpoint every 30 minutes.
2. For a 1-2 week iterative fine-tune: RunPod Community Cloud H100 SXM at $2.69/GPU-hr or Lambda 1x H100 PCIe at $3.29/GPU-hr. Per-second billing lets you stop and restart cheaply.
3. For a 1-3 month training run you can't afford to lose: Lambda Reserved Cloud 16-GPU cluster at $6.16/GPU-hr, or Together AI reserved at $3.09/GPU-hr with commitment.
4. For a 200+ GPU distributed training job: CoreWeave HGX H100 with reserved negotiation. The 8-GPU node minimum and InfiniBand interconnect pay for themselves at scale; naive scaling on a cheaper cluster runs at 70% efficiency and costs more per useful FLOP.
5. For production inference with compliance requirements: AWS Capacity Blocks at $5.191/GPU-hr, or AWS 3-year reserved at $5-$6/GPU-hr. The integration with SageMaker and enterprise support justify the premium.

...

## What to watch next

Three near-term datapoints. First, the CoreWeave Q3 2026 earnings call — CoreWeave CFO stated the company is 'largely sold out' of 2026 capacity and raising list prices; expect rate-card increases by Q4 2026. Second, AWS's planned p6-b200.48xlarge at $98.84/hr effective — Blackwell-generation capacity will relieve H100 demand pressure and likely pull H100 list rates down 10-15% by mid-2027. Third, NVIDIA Vera Rubin full production at CoreWeave, Google, Azure, OCI, and Nebius — Rubin GPUs hit $40B/gigawatt revenue per NVIDIA's earnings, and as Rubin capacity comes online, H100 spot prices will fall faster than reserved rates (NVIDIA Q2 FY27 earnings, August 26, 2026).

results.title: Nebius Raises GPU Rental Prices 21% Amid AI Infrastructure Demand Surge | Gate News
highlights:
2026-09-22 06:23:26

- Nebius announced GPU rental price increases of 21% starting October 1, 2024 following June's 30% hike.
- Nebius's B300 on-demand rental price increased 56% cumulatively over five months total.
- Oracle renewed all expired GPU contracts at 20% higher rates during its previous quarter.

GPU rental provider Nebius announced it will raise on-demand GPU rental prices by up to 21% starting October 1, according to a September 22 report by Eugene Investment & Securities analyst Park Jae-hwan. The increase follows a 30% price hike across all GPU lineups on June 1, bringing Nebius's B300 on-demand rental price to a 56% increase over approximately five months. Eugene Investment attributes the sustained price escalation to robust AI infrastructure demand amid intensifying competition among AI model developers, with Oracle similarly renewing all expired GPU contracts at 20% higher rates in its previous quarter.

## Nebius Implements Second GPU Price Increase in Five Months

Nebius decided to raise GPU on-demand rental prices by up to 21% effective October 1, marking the second increase since June 1 when the company raised prices by 30% across its entire GPU lineup. Park Jae-hwan noted that Nebius's B300 on-demand rental price has risen approximately 56% over about five months as a result of these consecutive adjustments.

## Oracle Renews GPU Contracts at 20% Premium

The rental price trend extends beyond Nebius. Oracle disclosed during its previous quarter earnings announcement that it renewed and resold all expired GPU contracts at prices 20% higher than previous rates. Park stated that the simultaneous reflection of rental price increases in both spot and contract pricing suggests accelerating revenue growth for neo-cloud companies and reconfirms the strength of AI infrastructure demand.

results.title: Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs
highlights:
A virtualized compute environment creates opportunities for both cloud providers and their customers. One is preemptible VMs (PVMs): interruptible compute for non-critical workloads that runs on pre-allocated, temporarily idle capacity. For the GPU compute market, which is still dealing with a scarcity problem, this distribution model presents an elegant solution. Today, we’re introducing dynamic spot pricing for PVMs: an algorithm that reads available capacity and real-time demand signals from Nebius users to set the price automatically.

We launched preemptible VMs last year and they’ve become popular among our customers. Customers use PVMs to complete non-critical tasks like data processing, experimentation, and short fine-tuning jobs, significantly cutting their GPU compute costs. Despite their short-term nature, most of our users finish their jobs and shut down their VMs themselves, or the VM shuts down automatically if they use Serverless AI. In our experience, only a small fraction of PVM workloads are interrupted by capacity reclamation.

...

## How spot pricing works How spot pricing works

The spot pricing system aggregates information about existing capacity and demand signals from Nebius customers, then calculates a spot price for preemptible VMs on a specific GPU type in a specific region. The spot price changes over time and cannot fall below a set price floor. There is no upper limit, so during periods of high demand the spot price can rise above the on-demand GPU-hour rate.

Note

Update, November 2, 2026: this section previously stated that the spot price always stays between a floor and a ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate. We have removed the ceiling. Customers can cap what they pay by setting a max price.

Recent spot price changes, up to 30 days back, are shown in the pricing history diagram. This view is intended to help customers identify typical demand and pricing patterns, so they can make informed decisions about how to time their future PVM consumption.

To see the current spot price, customers can simply create a compute instance and select a preemptible virtual machine. The price is currently updated up to every 15 minutes and is the same for every resource type that runs on preemptible capacity, including Kubernetes clusters and Serverless AI.

...

Spot pricing gives Nebius AI Cloud users two strategies from which to choose.

Chase the best price: To adopt this strategy, the customer creates a pricing policy that sets a max price: the highest amount per GPU-hour they are willing to pay, based on GPU type and region (see Figure 3). When the spot price is at or below the max price, the workload runs and the user pays the spot price. If the spot price exceeds the max price, the instance is stopped, data is retained, and the PVM can be restarted once the price comes back below the desired max price. Standalone VMs don’t restart on their own: restart them manually, or automate this via Terraform, SDK, API, or CLI. Kubernetes restarts preemptible VMs in your clusters automatically.

Follow the trend: This strategy prioritizes maximizing the chances of keeping the workload running. If a customer chooses to follow the spot price rather than set a max price when creating a compute resource, that resource is charged at the dynamic spot price, and the customer loses access to their preemptible VM only due to maintenance events or if this capacity is reclaimed.

...

You can start using preemptible VMs today, and the new tooling and settings are already available. Dynamic pricing itself takes effect on 8 October. If you already use preemptible resources, you’ll need to configure a price setting for them before that date. Look out for an email with more information.

results.title: Ask three GPU providers for a price and you'll get three answers, each shaped by how much you're buying, how long you're committing for, and how well you already know what the …
highlights:
Ask three GPU providers for a price and you'll get three answers, each shaped by how much you're buying, how long you're committing for, and how well you already know what the number should be. Published rates are a starting position. The real price gets negotiated.

That works if you have leverage. It works much less well if you're buying compute for the first time, with no reference point for what a good number looks like.

Nobody designed it this way. It's where the market happens to be, and I don't think it has to stay there.

Spot pricing for preemptible VMs is a first step. The rate is calculated from available capacity and demand rather than set internally, and it's published with its recent history so customers can see how it forms.

One product, one class of capacity. But it's the direction we're building toward.

...

**Prem Naraindas** · 2026-09-22T00:00:00+00:00
> Publishing the rate with its history is the half of this I would push furthest, because price is only half the buyer's problem. The other half is that a first-time buyer has no way to turn a GPU hour into the number their CFO actually asks for, which is the cost of serving one request in production. That number is decided by utilisation, and utilisation is decided by how the workload is scheduled, not by the rate card. Transparency on price makes the market fairer. Transparency on utilisation is what would let a regulated buyer compare renting with running, which is the decision most of them are actually making this year.
